note: Rav Safra was in a bathroom when Rabbi Abba came by and coughed to ask whether he might come in. Rav Safra told him: Enter, Master. When Rav Safra came out, Rabbi Abba rebuked him: you have never been to Seir, yet you have learned the ways of Seir. Did the mishna not teach that a closed door shows someone is inside, meaning that no one should go in while another person is there?
why: The mishna describes a dignified bathroom in the Temple whose closed door showed it was in use. The Gemara then defends Rav Safra: he feared Rabbi Abba's health would be at risk if he had to hold back.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Invites Rabbi Abba into the bathroom while he is inside.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Enters at Rav Safra's invitation and then rebukes him for it.

terms.meaning: The land of the Edomites; here a byword for people who behave immodestly.

note: A man drank water and, without pouring some out first, handed the cup to his student. The student was a fastidious person and would not drink from it, and he died of thirst. At that time the Sages ruled that a person should not drink water and give the rest to his student unless he first pours some of it out.
why: Rav and Rav Huna have just told their sons to pour out a little water before passing the cup to a student; this baraita gives the incident behind that advice. Rav Ashi draws from it that a student who pours out water in front of his teacher is not being disrespectful.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Concludes that a student may pour out water in front of his teacher without disrespect.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

note: Two priests were tied as they raced up the altar ramp. One of them shoved the other, and his leg was broken. When the court saw that people were coming into danger, they ruled that the ashes would be removed from the altar only by lottery.
why: The Gemara is reconciling two clauses of the mishna: in one, the first priest ready removes the ashes; in the other, a lottery decides. Abaye says the first describes practice before the lottery was enacted, and this incident is why it was enacted.

terms.meaning: The first Temple task each morning, clearing ashes from the altar; priests competed for the honor.
The sloping walkway priests climbed to reach the top of the altar.

note: Alexander of Macedon put ten questions to the Elders of the Negev: whether heaven to earth or east to west is farther, whether heaven or earth was created first, whether light or darkness came first, who is wise, mighty and rich, how a man lives and dies, how to win people's favor, and whether to live at sea or on land. They answered all but the question on light and darkness. When he called their united stand opposition and threatened to kill them, they told him falsehood does not suit a king, and he dressed them in purple with gold chains. He set out for Africa, crossed the Mountains of Darkness on their advice, and reached a town of women, who brought him bread of gold on a golden table. How that meeting ends is not given here.
why: The Gemara has just explained that the daily offering was slaughtered facing the sun. It brings Alexander's questions because his first one concerns the sun's place in the sky.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: A king who questions the Elders of the Negev and then sets out to conquer Africa.

people.name: the Elders of the Negev
people.about: The Sages Alexander questions, who answer him and advise him on his journey.

terms.meaning: A mountain range the Elders say blocks the way to Africa, which can be crossed only with animals that walk in the dark.
Here, the force that leads people to do what is plainly wrong; the Elders say even it sometimes wins.

flag: Breaks off mid-scene: the women's reply about the golden bread and Alexander's lesson fall in the AFTER segment (they open story AB7901).

note: Alexander asked the women whether people eat bread of gold. They replied that if he only wanted bread, he had bread at home; that was not why he had come. On leaving, he wrote on the town gate: I, Alexander of Macedon, was a fool until I came to the land of Africa of women, and I learned sense from women. Later, eating salted fish by a spring, he smelled a fragrance and concluded the spring came from the Garden of Eden. Some say he followed it to Eden's gate and demanded entry; refused, he asked for something, and was given an eyeball that outweighed all his gold and silver. The Sages told him the human eye is never satisfied, and once he covered it with dirt, it balanced.
why: This continues the Gemara's account of Alexander, which began with his questions to the Elders of the Negev and his march to Africa. After it, the Gemara adds a teaching that Gehenna lies beyond the Mountains of Darkness he crossed.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: A king on campaign in Africa, who learns from a town of women and seeks entry to the Garden of Eden.

terms.meaning: Paradise, the garden of the first humans; here its gate is guarded and only the righteous may enter.
